newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan recovery seems slow but tangible - economists.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan recovery seems slow but tangible - economists.

text.p: Taiwan's latest economic indicators have convinced most economists that a long-awaited recovery is real and even accelerating but still slower than the government had hoped, analysts said on Tuesday.
"The recovery is clear now and is gradually strengthening, but probably is still slower than the government's expectation," Nomura Securities economist Amy Huang said on Tuesday.
The tempered expectations are the result of a mixed batch of fresh economic statistics.

Industrial output in December rose 6.11 percent compared to December 1995, chiefly on the strength of recovering second-half manufacturing, the Economics Ministry said on Tuesday. The figure was sharply above the average 2.99 percent projection compiled from a Reuters poll of Taiwan economists last week.
However, December export orders rose a mere 0.96 percent year-on-year, well below the average 1.64 percent projection in the same Reuters poll.
Taiwan's economy, beset by icy relations with China and sluggish performances in several manufacturing sectors, has slumped since late 1995.

The island's gross domestic product (GDP) growth dropped to 6.03 percent that year, its lowest since 1990 and a far cry from the double-digit levels of the 1980s. The government has predicted even lower growth of 5.70 percent for 1996.
Most economists expect slow GDP growth in 1997. Private economists have forecast growth of between 5.70 and 6.20 percent, against the latest government forecast of 6.20 percent.
But economists disagree on what will fuel the recovery.
Some feel government pledges to accelerate public works projects will translate into greater domestic demand that could kindle a revival.
"With the state's decision to speed the progress of public construction projects, 1997 domestic demand should rise stronger than export growth," said Nomura's Huang.
Huang said she expected industrial output -- boosted mainly by domestic demand -- to rise 5.6 percent in calendar 1997, a sharp recovery from actual 1996 output growth of 1.70 percent.
But Capital Securities economist Wang Chia-yuan was cautious.
"Whether domestic demand can be so strong as expected and whether the government can really accelerate infrastructure projects to boost demand remains to be seen," Wang said.

Wang said that although export growth has been slower than expected, exports might eventually emerge as the engine of any economic recovery. He cited recent growth in manufacturing output and a rebound in exports to Hong Kong, mainly involving goods destined for China, since November.
But most economists agreed Taiwan's economy would continue to recover in 1997, albeit slowly due to the sluggish revival in exports.
"Seeing December's mixed performance, I would say the trend of slow recovery hasn't changed," said National Securities economist Lin Kuo-yang.
Taiwan's export orders grew 4.76 percent in 1996. Various recent official and private forecasts have estimated 1997 export growth at around 5.0-8.0 percent.

"This year's export growth definitely will be better than in 1996 and we will see apparent growth starting from the second quarter," said Chang Yao-tsung, director of the Economics Ministry's statistics department.

Chang said his forecast was based mainly on a ministry survey showing that 28 percent of 1,559 local manufacturers interviewed believed 1997 exports would be better than 1996, up from 13 percent in a similar survey a year ago.
